question: Which correctly describes the structure of a typical 1-bit DRAM memory cell?
choices: One transistor and one capacitor
Six transistors
One transistor with a floating gate
explanation: A DRAM cell consists of one transistor and one capacitor (1T1C) and stores one bit according to whether the capacitor is charged. Six transistors is the SRAM cell, and a floating-gate transistor is the flash memory cell.

question: Why does DRAM need periodic refresh operations?
choices: To increase read speed
Because the number of writes is limited
Because the charge stored in the capacitor is gradually lost through leakage current
explanation: The charge stored in a DRAM capacitor is gradually lost through leakage currents in the transistor and junctions. Refresh reads and rewrites the data at regular intervals (generally within tens of milliseconds) before it is lost. A limited number of writes is a characteristic of flash memory.

question: Which correctly describes the read operation of DRAM?
choices: Reading does not change the cell's charge at all
Reading changes the cell's charge, so the data is amplified by a sense amplifier and written back to the cell
Reading uses tunneling current at high voltage
explanation: In DRAM, connecting the cell capacitor to the bit line shares its charge with the bit line, destroying the original state (destructive read). The sense amplifier therefore amplifies the tiny voltage difference to determine the data and at the same time writes the amplified value back to the cell.

question: Which pair of three-dimensional structures has been used in DRAM cells to secure capacitor capacitance?
choices: Fin and planar
Trench and stacked
Floating gate and charge trap
explanation: To secure enough capacitance as cells shrink, DRAM capacitors have been made three-dimensional. There are trench capacitors, formed by etching deep holes into the substrate, and stacked capacitors, built as tall structures above the transistor; stacked capacitors are now mainstream. Floating gate and charge trap are flash memory structures.

question: Which correctly describes a property of DRAM?
choices: It is volatile memory that loses data when the power is turned off
It is non-volatile memory that retains data when the power is turned off
It is read-only memory that cannot be rewritten
explanation: DRAM stores information as charge on a capacitor and is volatile: when power is turned off, the charge is not maintained and the data is lost. Even with power on, the charge gradually leaks away, so refresh is needed. Non-volatile memories such as flash retain data without power.

question: What does 'DDR (double data rate)' in DDR SDRAM mean?
choices: Data is transferred on both the rising and falling edges of the clock
Two DRAM chips are stacked
It operates at twice the supply voltage
explanation: DDR transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock, achieving twice the data rate at the same clock frequency. With each generation (DDR2, DDR3, DDR4, DDR5), transfer rates have increased and supply voltages have decreased.

question: In a DRAM cell array, which line connects to the gates of the cell transistors and selects the row to be read or written?
choices: Bit line
Word line
Power line
explanation: In a DRAM cell array, the word line selects a row and turns on the cell transistors, and the capacitor charge is read or written through the bit line. The bit line leads to a sense amplifier.

question: How does the data retention time of DRAM cells generally change as temperature rises?
choices: It gets longer
It does not change
It gets shorter
explanation: As temperature rises, junction leakage current increases and the capacitor charge is lost faster, so retention time gets shorter. For this reason, DRAM standards include provisions for shortening the refresh interval at high temperatures.

question: Which correctly describes a soft error in memory?
choices: An error in which stored data is temporarily flipped by radiation or the like, without damaging the device
A permanent failure due to a wiring defect during manufacturing
A failure in which the device breaks down due to aging
explanation: A soft error occurs when alpha particles from package materials or neutrons originating from cosmic rays generate charge in silicon and flip stored data. The device itself is not damaged, so rewriting the data restores normal operation. Error-correcting codes (ECC) and similar measures are used.

question: Compared with SRAM, which is a characteristic of DRAM?
choices: It is faster than SRAM and needs no refresh
Its cells are small and the cost per bit is low, but it needs refresh
It retains data when the power is turned off
explanation: DRAM is made of small 1T1C cells, so it is easier to make in large capacities than 6T SRAM and has a lower cost per bit. On the other hand, it needs refresh and is slower than SRAM, so DRAM is used for main memory and SRAM for caches.

question: Which correctly describes redundancy repair, used to improve DRAM yield?
choices: Rows or columns containing defective cells are replaced with spare rows or columns prepared in advance
All chips containing defective cells are discarded
The supply voltage is raised to make defective cells work
explanation: In large-capacity memory such as DRAM, discarding a whole chip because of a few defective cells would greatly reduce yield. Spare rows and columns are therefore provided, and defective locations found in testing are switched to spares using fuses or similar means.

question: What does an error-correcting code (ECC) used in memory do?
choices: Compresses data to increase capacity
Adds redundant bits to data to detect and correct bit errors
Encrypts data
explanation: ECC adds check bits to data so that errors can be detected and corrected when the data is read. To reduce the impact of soft errors and defects due to scaling, ECC is used in server memory, and DDR5 also builds ECC into the chip itself.

question: In DRAM, why is access time shorter when the same row (page) is accessed repeatedly?
choices: Because refresh is no longer needed
Because the supply voltage rises
Because the data of an activated row is held in the sense amplifiers and can be read by just switching columns
explanation: In DRAM, activating a row reads the data of all cells in that row into the sense amplifiers. Data in the same row can be read just by changing the column address without reactivating the row, so access is faster. Memory controllers use this property to optimize the order of accesses.

question: Why are high-k materials such as zirconium oxide used for the dielectric film of DRAM capacitors?
choices: To secure the necessary capacitance in a small area
To reduce wiring resistance
To make the capacitor emit light
explanation: Capacitance is proportional to permittivity. Even as cells shrink, a certain capacitance is needed to read data correctly, so high-k materials such as ZrO2, with higher permittivity than SiO2, are used to obtain the needed capacitance in a small area.

question: Which correctly describes the self-refresh mode of DRAM?
choices: A mode that erases all data
A mode in which the DRAM refreshes itself internally without external commands, retaining data at low power, for example during standby
A mode that doubles access speed
explanation: In self-refresh mode, the DRAM refreshes itself using an internal timer. Because no commands are needed from the memory controller, data can be retained at low power, for example while a smartphone or PC is asleep.

question: How much is an 8 Gbit DRAM chip in bytes?
choices: 1 GB
8 GB
64 GB
explanation: One byte is 8 bits, so 8 Gbit ÷ 8 = 1 GB. Memory chip capacity is usually given in bits, while memory module capacity is usually given in bytes. For example, eight 8 Gbit chips make an 8 GB module.

question: What does the CAS latency (CL) of DRAM mean?
choices: The refresh interval
The number of clock cycles from a read command (specifying the column address) until data is output
The supply voltage of the DRAM
explanation: CAS latency is the number of clock cycles from receiving a read command that specifies the column address until the first data is output. A smaller value means a faster response, but the actual time is the product with the clock period, so faster-clocked standards have larger CL numbers.

question: What is the main use of the DRAM standard called LPDDR?
choices: Exclusively for large servers
Recording on optical discs
Devices that require low power, such as smartphones
explanation: LPDDR (low-power DDR) is a mobile DRAM standard that reduces power with lower supply voltages, power-saving modes and other features. It is used in smartphones, tablets and thin laptops, and is sometimes stacked in the same package as the processor.

question: Which is a characteristic of GDDR, used as graphics memory for GPUs?
choices: It is a standard that emphasizes data transfer bandwidth (speed)
It retains data when the power is turned off
It is slow but very cheap
explanation: GDDR is a DRAM standard that emphasizes data transfer speed so that GPUs can handle large amounts of image data quickly. Its per-pin data rate is higher than ordinary DDR, and it is used in graphics cards and game consoles. When even more bandwidth is needed, HBM is used.

question: What is the main purpose of burying the gate electrode in a trench in the silicon substrate (buried word line) in recent DRAM cell transistors?
choices: To make the cell emit light
To lengthen the effective channel and suppress leakage while shrinking the cell
To eliminate the need for a capacitor
explanation: DRAM cell transistors need extremely low leakage so that the capacitor charge does not escape. Burying the gate in a trench allows a longer effective channel along the trench even with small planar dimensions, suppressing leakage due to short-channel effects.

question: In DRAM, what is the main reason for splitting the address into row and column addresses and supplying them in turn through the same pins?
choices: To reduce the number of address pins
To eliminate the need for refresh
To encrypt the data
explanation: DRAM has a large capacity, so supplying the whole address at once would require many pins. Supplying the row and column addresses through the same pins at different times (address multiplexing) reduces the number of pins. It also matches DRAM's internal operation of activating a row and then selecting a column.

question: What is the main purpose of dividing the inside of a DRAM into multiple banks?
choices: To reduce capacity
To overlap operations in different banks and improve effective access performance
To increase heat generation
explanation: Activating and precharging a DRAM row takes time. With multiple banks, one bank can be accessed while another performs these operations, hiding the wait time and improving overall transfer efficiency.

question: Why is the voltage change on the bit line very small when DRAM is read?
choices: Because the supply voltage is very high
Because the bit line resistance is zero
Because the cell capacitor's capacitance is much smaller than the bit line's parasitic capacitance
explanation: During a read, the cell capacitor's charge is shared with the bit line. The cell capacitance is much smaller than the bit line capacitance, so the bit line voltage changes only slightly (tens to around a hundred-odd mV). The sense amplifier amplifies this small change to decide 0 or 1.

question: Which correctly describes the idea of 3D DRAM, under research and development as a way to increase future DRAM capacity?
choices: Stacking memory cells vertically to increase capacity without relying only on planar scaling
Increasing capacity just by making the chip larger
Replacing DRAM with SRAM
explanation: Planar scaling of DRAM is becoming difficult, so 3D DRAM, which stacks memory cells vertically like 3D NAND, is under research and development. Structures that lay the capacitors and transistors horizontally and stack them are being considered.

question: In DRAM, what is the phenomenon in which repeatedly activating one row in a short time can flip data in adjacent rows?
choices: Soft error
Row hammer
Latch-up
explanation: Row hammer is a phenomenon in which repeatedly activating the word line of one row makes cells in adjacent rows lose charge more easily, flipping their data. It became apparent as scaling brought cells closer together and also became a security issue. Countermeasures include extra refreshes for rows next to frequently accessed ones.

question: Which correctly describes the main leakage paths that determine the data retention time of DRAM cells?
choices: Subthreshold leakage of the cell transistor and junction leakage
Charge generated by light
Charge moved by magnetic fields
explanation: The charge on a DRAM capacitor is lost mainly through subthreshold leakage when the cell transistor is off and through leakage at the storage-node junction (including GIDL). Reducing these extends retention time and lowers refresh frequency and power.

question: What does F mean in '6F²', used to express DRAM cell area?
choices: Farad (the unit of capacitance)
The number of fins
The minimum feature size
explanation: F represents the minimum feature size, and cell area is expressed as a multiple of F squared. 6F² means an area six times the square of the minimum feature size. DRAM cell structures have improved from 8F² to 6F², and research aims to achieve 4F².

question: In DRAM access, what is the operation called that closes the open row and returns the bit lines to an intermediate voltage to prepare for activating the next row?
choices: Refresh
Precharge
Erase
explanation: Before accessing a different row, DRAM must precharge: close the current row and return the bit lines to an intermediate voltage. This time is included in access latency, so its impact is reduced by increasing consecutive accesses to the same row and by using multiple banks.

question: Which function, adopted in DDR5, corrects errors inside the DRAM chip?
choices: On-die ECC
Wear leveling
TRIM
explanation: To cope with more cell defects and errors due to scaling, DDR5 builds an error-correction circuit into the DRAM chip itself (on-die ECC). Separate from system-level ECC, it corrects single-bit errors and similar errors inside the chip.

question: What is the performance limitation called that arises because improvements in memory bandwidth and latency have not kept up with improvements in processor performance?
choices: Moore's law
Silicon cycle
Memory wall
explanation: Processor computing performance has improved greatly, but DRAM access latency and bandwidth have not improved as much, so time spent waiting for data has come to limit performance. This is called the memory wall. Larger caches and high-bandwidth memories such as HBM are responses to it.
